add_eyes.name: Nella Larsen
add_eyes.role: Novelist, aged about 37 when Quicksand appeared; trained nurse and former children's librarian at the 135th Street branch of the New York Public Library
add_eyes.side: Danish and West Indian parentage; Harlem's literary society
add_eyes.where: Harlem, and the downtown parties of Van Vechten and Marinoff
add_eyes.vantage_label: the novelist between Harlem and downtown
add_eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Van Vechten and Marinoff are in the Carl Van Vechten Papers at Yale's Beinecke Library; most are headed only with a weekday, so editors date them by content, in square brackets. A further small collection is at the New York Public Library. One letter was published in full by Fabi and McLendon (RSAJournal 25, 2014). Twentieth-century letters: digest only.
add_eyes.bio: Larsen published two short novels, Quicksand (1928) and Passing (1929), about women caught between colour lines, and dedicated the second to Van Vechten and his wife. Du Bois praised Quicksand in the same review in which he condemned McKay's Home to Harlem. Her letters show a writer who promoted herself and mocked herself in the same paragraph, and who moved more freely between Harlem and white literary New York than almost anyone in the chapter.

sources.title: Fabi and McLendon, 'Though years have flown by': A Letter from Nella Larsen to Carl Van Vechten (RSAJournal, 2014)
NY1920: Nella Larsen's application to library school

add_eyes.name: Paulette Nardal
add_eyes.role: Martinican journalist and translator in Paris, aged 35 in 1931; with her sisters, host of a Sunday salon at Clamart; founding editor of La Revue du monde noir
add_eyes.vantage_label: abroad: Harlem read and translated in Paris
add_eyes.form: published essays and an edited bilingual review (dated monthly issues)
add_eyes.authenticity: The six issues of La Revue du monde noir (November 1931 – April 1932) survive and are digitised in several libraries. Her own essays, including 'Awakening of Race Consciousness', are signed. No diary is known. Twentieth-century material: digest only.
add_eyes.bio: From the late 1920s Paulette Nardal and her sisters held a salon at Clamart where McKay, Alain Locke and Countee Cullen met African and Caribbean students in Paris, among them the young Césaire, Senghor and Damas. Her bilingual review printed Hughes, McKay and Walter White beside Antillean and Haitian writers. It closes the chapter's arc in Paris, where the Harlem writers' work fed what became négritude.

sources.title: Modernist Magazines Project: La Revue du monde noir
Princeton DPUL: La Revue du monde noir

add_eyes.name: Marcus Garvey and the Negro World (UNIA weekly)
add_eyes.role: The weekly newspaper of Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, then the largest-circulation Black paper in the movement's orbit; Garvey wrote its front-page editorials from prison and later from Jamaica
add_eyes.where: Negro World office, Harlem; Garvey in the Atlanta penitentiary 1925–27, then Kingston, Jamaica
add_eyes.vantage_label: the rival Black press, outside the NAACP circle
add_eyes.language: English (with Spanish and French sections at times)
add_eyes.authenticity: Surviving issues are held by the Schomburg Center and other libraries, and the key texts are edited with full dates in Robert A. Hill (ed.), The Marcus Garvey and UNIA Papers (UCLA). A collective eye like a press record, not a diary. Twentieth-century texts: digest only.
add_eyes.bio: The Negro World carried poetry and book reviews as well as politics, and Claude McKay wrote for it in 1919–20. The paper and the NAACP's Crisis attacked each other for years. It gives the chapter the voice of a mass movement that wanted a Black nation more than a literary renaissance, and judged the novels of Harlem by whether they insulted the race.

sources.title: UCLA, Marcus Garvey Papers: American Series introduction (vol. VII)
NYPL Digital Collections: The Negro World
Letters from London in Black and Red: Claude McKay, Marcus Garvey and the Negro World (Project MUSE)

add_entries.place: Algonquin Hotel, a Ceylonese restaurant, and the 63rd Street theatre, Manhattan
add_entries.headline: A cold, an essay posted, and the premiere of Liza
add_entries.digest: Nursing a cold, Van Vechten noted posting an essay to Emily Clark for The Reviewer and lunching at the Algonquin with Fania Marinoff and a friend. After dinner the two went to the opening of Liza, the Black musical with Gertrude Saunders that followed Shuffle Along into the same 63rd Street theatre. Two years before he met Hughes, the daybook already shows him going to Black shows.
add_entries.source_note: Van Vechten, The Splendid Drunken Twenties: Selections from the Daybooks, 1922–1930, ed. Bruce Kellner (2003), entry for 27 November 1922, as excerpted by The Diary Junction blog (digest only).

add_entries.headline: Hurston is the most amusing person he knows
add_entries.digest: A month after the Opportunity dinner where Hurston made her entrance, Van Vechten wrote to his wife that she was one of the most amusing people he had met. He was already bringing her downtown, and she in turn named him and Fannie Hurst among the 'Negrotarians', her word for the white friends of the movement.
add_entries.source_note: Letter of 3 June 1925, cited in a footnote of 'Enter the Negrotarians', S&F Online (Barnard). This is a letter, not a daybook entry.

add_entries.headline: Larsen tells Charles S. Johnson what she reads
add_entries.digest: In a letter to Charles S. Johnson of Opportunity, dated by editors to August 1926, Larsen said she preferred European writers and the American moderns. She was then writing her first novel and placing herself among cosmopolitan modernists rather than in the folk tradition being promoted uptown.
add_entries.source_note: Fabi and McLendon, RSAJournal 25 (2014), citing Larsen to C. S. Johnson, n.d. [Aug. 1926]; the date is an editorial inference.

add_entries.headline: Quicksand is published
add_entries.digest: Knopf published Larsen's first novel, about Helga Crane, a woman of mixed Danish and Black parentage who moves from a Southern school to Harlem, Copenhagen and finally a rural Southern marriage. It appeared within weeks of McKay's Home to Harlem, and reviewers set the two side by side.
add_entries.source_note: Year confirmed (RSAJournal 2014; SNAC). Month as usually given in Larsen chronologies; not checked against a dated review this session.

add_entries.headline: Asking Van Vechten's help with a prize application
add_entries.digest: Larsen wrote to Van Vechten about her application for the Harmon Foundation's award in literature. Fabi and McLendon read the letter as balancing self-promotion with self-criticism, a tone they find in her letters generally.
add_entries.source_note: Fabi and McLendon, RSAJournal 25 (2014), on Larsen's comments to Van Vechten about her 1928 Harmon application (year only).

add_entries.headline: A Harmon bronze medal for Quicksand
add_entries.digest: The Harmon Foundation gave Larsen its bronze medal, the second award in literature, for Quicksand. The Harmon awards, judged largely by white panels, were by then one of the few sources of money and notice for Black writers outside the magazine contests.
add_entries.source_note: Fabi and McLendon, RSAJournal 25 (2014), note 3 (bronze medal, second place, 1929).

add_entries.headline: Passing, dedicated to Van Vechten and Marinoff
add_entries.digest: Larsen's second novel, the story of two childhood friends, one of whom passes as white and is married to a racist, came out from Knopf. Larsen had discussed the manuscript with Van Vechten under a provocative working title, and she dedicated the book to him and Fania Marinoff.
add_entries.source_note: Dedication and the letters about the working title: RSAJournal 25 (2014). Year confirmed; month as usually given, not verified this session.

add_entries.headline: Garvey deported, and still writing the front page
add_entries.digest: After his prison sentence was commuted, Garvey was deported from New Orleans and landed in Jamaica on 10 December 1927. From Kingston he went on sending editorials to the Negro World, and their themes began to change. The paper remained in Harlem without him.
add_entries.source_note: Hill (ed.), Marcus Garvey and UNIA Papers, American Series introduction (UCLA): deportation December 1927, arrival 10 December; editorials after deportation.

add_entries.headline: The paper insists Garvey still leads
add_entries.digest: With Garvey abroad, the Negro World printed a statement by the UNIA organiser Samuel Haynes calling him the movement's supreme leader. It was a week-by-week struggle to hold a mass movement together, carried on a few blocks from the parties and salons in this chapter.
add_entries.source_note: UCLA Marcus Garvey Papers, American Series introduction (issue of 14 January 1928 cited).

add_entries.headline: Garvey condemns Home to Harlem
add_entries.digest: Garvey reviewed McKay's best-seller in the Negro World and called it a libel on the race. He charged McKay, who had once written for the paper, and others with painting Black life as vice and cabaret for white buyers. His attack echoed Du Bois's of June, though the two men agreed on little else.
add_entries.source_note: Review widely cited in McKay scholarship (often as Negro World, 29 September 1928); the issue and wording were not seen this session, so the month is approximate.

add_entries.headline: Garvey stops writing for his own paper
add_entries.digest: In autumn 1931 Garvey stopped contributing to the Negro World, and in July 1932 he disowned it. The paper carried on with dwindling money until it closed in October 1933, outliving the Renaissance's boom years only briefly.
add_entries.source_note: UCLA Marcus Garvey Papers, American Series introduction (fall 1931; July 1932; October 1933). The season is given, not a day.

add_entries.headline: La Revue du monde noir: Harlem in two languages
add_entries.digest: Nardal and the Haitian Léo Sajous brought out the first issue of a bilingual monthly in French and English, conceived at the Clamart salon. Over its run it printed Hughes's 'I, Too', poems by McKay, an extract from Walter White and a drawing by Aaron Douglas beside work by Antillean, Haitian and African writers. It appeared in the year of the Paris Colonial Exposition.
add_entries.source_note: Modernist Magazines Project (first issue November 1931; editors; bilingual; Harlem contributors); La Vie des idées (salon at 7 rue Hébert; Exposition coloniale opened 6 May 1931).

add_entries.headline: Six issues, then silence; 'Awakening of Race Consciousness'
add_entries.digest: The review ended with its sixth issue after a political controversy cost it its funding. In her essay on the awakening of race consciousness Nardal traced how Antillean students in Paris had come to Black self-awareness, and credited Black American writers and scholars with showing the way. Césaire, Senghor and Damas would take the idea further as négritude.
add_entries.source_note: End of the run and loss of funds: Modernist Magazines Project; Princeton DPUL. The essay is signed by Nardal; that it appeared in the final (April 1932) issue is commonly stated but was not confirmed this session.

add_convergences.label: March–September 1928: two novels, three verdicts
add_convergences.note: Quicksand and Home to Harlem came out within weeks of each other. Du Bois praised Larsen and said McKay's book made him want to bathe; Garvey's paper, from the other side of the Black press, condemned McKay as well. McKay, in Barcelona, answered Du Bois only in a private letter of 13 June.

add_convergences.label: November 1931 – April 1932: Harlem in a Paris review
add_convergences.note: Nardal's bilingual monthly reprinted Hughes, McKay and a Douglas drawing for French-speaking readers, as the Renaissance's boom in New York ended with the Depression. The texts were Harlem's; the readers were the Antillean and African students of Clamart who would make négritude.

add_ties.note: Close friends and correspondents; she discussed Passing with him in manuscript and dedicated it to him and Fania Marinoff in 1929.
She wrote to Johnson about her reading in 1926, while Opportunity was the main forum for new Black fiction.
McKay was among the Harlem writers who visited the Nardal sisters' Clamart salon; his poems appeared in her review.

Garvey's Negro World and Du Bois's Crisis attacked each other for years; in 1924 Du Bois called Garvey either a lunatic or a traitor. In 1928 the two men nonetheless agreed in condemning Home to Harlem.

add_threads_out.note: Du Bois, who read Tagore, asked him for a message to Black Americans, and The Crisis printed Tagore's reply in 1929. In 1913 the New York press had noted that the Nobel Prize had gone for the first time to someone who was not white.

The federal art projects that followed George Biddle's 1933 appeal to Roosevelt, made in the name of Mexico's public murals, paid for Aaron Douglas's 'Aspects of Negro Life' (1934) at the Harlem branch library.

fix.form: daybooks (brief dated diary); dated letters; printed introductions and novel
fix.authenticity: His daybooks are true dated diaries, kept in brief daily notes; selections were published as The Splendid Drunken Twenties: Selections from the Daybooks, 1922–1930, ed. Bruce Kellner (University of Illinois Press, 2003). The 27 November 1922 entry used here is taken from a published excerpt of that edition; other entries rest on his dated letters and his signed introduction to The Weary Blues. His papers are chiefly at Yale's Beinecke Library, with a further collection at the New York Public Library. His famous portrait photographs date from 1932 onward, after this chapter. Published 2003: digest only.
